title: There was a season when Absalom looked untouchable.
paragraphs: There was a season when Absalom looked untouchable.

Handsome. Charismatic. Royal blood flowing through his veins. The kind of man who could walk into a room and instantly pull attention without speaking a word. Scripture says there was “no blemish in him from head to foot” (2 Samuel 14:25). Israel admired him. Women desired him. Men respected him. Crowds followed him.
But buried inside the very verse that celebrated him… was the warning that would destroy him.
His hair.
The thing that made him glorious before men eventually became the instrument of his judgment before God.
And that is how sin works.
The thing you worship eventually becomes the thing that traps you.
The story of Absalom is not just ancient history. It is a mirror. A terrifying one.
Because many people today are hanging from the very thing they used to boast about.

Their beauty.
Their influence.
Their intelligence.
Their money.
Their body.
Their status.
Their platform.
Their pride.
Absalom’s hair became his curse because Absalom himself became consumed with Absalom.
The Hebrew text in 2 Samuel 14:26 says:
“וּבְגַלְּחוֹ אֶת־רֹאשׁוֹ… וְשָׁקַל אֶת־שְׂעַר רֹאשׁוֹ”

Transliteration:
“U’v’gall’cho et rosho… v’shaqal et se’ar rosho.”

Literal meaning:
“When he cut the hair of his head… he weighed the hair of his head.”
This detail matters deeply.
Scripture says his hair weighed “two hundred shekels.”
Why would the Bible mention the weight of a man’s hair?
Because God was exposing the condition of Absalom’s heart.

The Hebrew word used for “weighed” is “שָׁקַל” (shaqal), meaning:
to measure,
to evaluate,
to value.
Absalom literally measured the thing he gloried in.
His identity became wrapped in external beauty instead of internal holiness.
He cultivated image more than character.
And eventually image without character becomes demonic vanity.
The tragedy of Absalom is not hair.
The tragedy is unchecked pride.
Long before Absalom was hanging from a tree, he was already hanging spiritually.

Suspended between rebellion and repentance.
Close to the kingdom…
but far from God.
And that is the dangerous place many people live today.

Close to church.
Close to Christian language.
Close to worship music.
Close to ministry culture.
But their hearts are still enthroning themselves.
Absalom did not simply wake up one morning and become evil.
Bitterness slowly discipled him.

After Amnon violated Tamar, Absalom carried rage for years. Instead of surrendering pain to God, he fed revenge privately. Eventually he murdered Amnon. Then he manipulated public opinion against his father David. Then he stole hearts politically at the city gate.
2 Samuel 15:6 says:
“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.”

The Hebrew phrase:
“וַיְגַנֵּב אַבְשָׁלוֹם אֶת־לֵב”
(Vay’gannev Avshalom et-lev)
“Stole the hearts.”

The word “gannev” means:
to secretly steal,
to deceive,
to carry away subtly.
Absalom mastered appearances.

Outwardly compassionate.
Inwardly ambitious.
He kissed people while plotting rebellion.
And this is why external attractiveness without surrendered character is dangerous.
Because charisma can fool crowds while corruption grows underneath.
Then came the final moment.

The moment many people know…
but few truly understand.
2 Samuel 18:9 says Absalom was riding through the forest on a mule when his head became caught in the branches of a great oak tree.
The Hebrew says:

“וַיֵּאָחֵז רֹאשׁוֹ בָּאֵלָה”
(Vaye’achez rosho ba’elah)
“His head was seized in the oak.”
Notice this carefully.
The text does not even primarily emphasize the hair.
It emphasizes the head.

The seat of pride.
Authority.
Identity.
Self-exaltation.
Jewish tradition and many ancient commentators connected this event to his thick hair because the narrative intentionally emphasized it earlier.
The very glory Absalom cultivated became the mechanism that immobilized him.
The forest did what no army could do.
It grabbed the thing he prized most.
And suddenly the beautiful prince became helpless.
Suspended between heaven and earth.
Rejected by both.
The imagery is horrifying.
A man once adored by crowds now dangling in humiliation.
A man who wanted a throne now hanging from a tree.
A man obsessed with appearance now exposed publicly.
Sin always promises elevation before delivering humiliation.
The Greek translation in the Septuagint uses language implying he was “entangled.”
That word carries the idea of being ensnared or trapped.
Exactly what pride does.
Pride never feels dangerous in the beginning.
It feels empowering.

You feel superior.
Untouchable.
Entitled.
But eventually pride wraps around your soul like chains.

Lucifer fell through pride.
Nebuchadnezzar lost his sanity through pride.
Herod was struck down in pride.
And Absalom hung in pride.
God opposes the proud because pride competes with God Himself.
The terrifying reality is this:
Absalom still had royal blood while hanging from that tree.
He was still David’s son.
Position did not save him.
Heritage did not save him.
Potential did not save him.
Unrepented rebellion destroyed him.

There are people today depending on family Christianity.
Church attendance.
Ministry titles.
Religious language.
Online sermons.
Christian content.
But none of those things can replace surrender.
You can know worship culture and still be spiritually dying inside.
Absalom’s hair became his curse because the outward thing he glorified replaced inward submission to God.
And many modern believers are doing the same thing with different forms of “hair.”

Some worship aesthetics.
Some worship influence.
Some worship intellect.
Some worship political identity.
Some worship platforms.
Some worship image management.
Some worship self-expression more than holiness.
Anything exalted above obedience eventually becomes an idol.
And idols always become cruel masters.
What makes this story even more heartbreaking is David’s response.
When Absalom died, David wept:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee…”
The Hebrew repetition carries deep agony.

“בְּנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי”
(B’ni Avshalom, b’ni, v’ni)
“My son Absalom, my son, my son…”
This is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures foreshadowing the Gospel itself.
A father grieving over a rebellious son.
Except unlike David, Jesus actually did die for the rebellious.
The cross became the place where pride could finally be crucified.
Because humanity has an Absalom problem.
We all want our own throne.
We all naturally exalt self.
We all resist surrender.
Romans 3:23 in Greek says:

“πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον”
(Pantes gar hēmarton)
“For all have sinned.”

The word “hēmarton” means:
to miss the mark,
to fall short,
to deviate from God’s standard.
And pride sits underneath all sin.
But this is why the Gospel is so powerful.
Jesus did what Absalom refused to do.
Philippians 2 says Christ humbled Himself.
The Greek says:

“ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν”
(etapeínōsen heauton)
“He humbled Himself.”

Absalom exalted himself and was brought low.
Jesus humbled Himself and was exalted above every name.
That contrast changes everything.

One man clung to glory and died in rebellion.
The other released glory and died for rebels.
And now every human being must decide which path to follow.

The kingdom of self…
or the kingdom of God.
Maybe your “hair” is not physical beauty.

Maybe it is ego.
Control.
Bitterness.
Secret sin.
Validation addiction.
Pride disguised as confidence.
Performance Christianity.
A hidden rebellion nobody sees yet.
But if it is not surrendered to Christ, eventually it will begin wrapping around your soul.
Be honest.
What are you secretly measuring your worth by?
Because the thing you idolize today may become the thing that destroys you tomorrow.
And if you know someone trapped in image, ego, rebellion, bitterness, or secret pride, share this with them before it is too late.

Some people are not destroyed by what they suffer…
but by what they refuse to surrender.
